newsitem.title: UK: Options show market still sanguine about UK poll.
newsitem.headline: Options show market still sanguine about UK poll.

text.p: With just three days until Thursday's UK election, prices and activity in the sterling options market show investors still remarkably calm about the prospect of the first change in government here in 18 years.

Implied volatility levels, the market assumption of future currency volatility and the benchmark for options pricing, are expected to remain underpinned until after Thursday. But there is little or no sign of panic options positioning or any frantic last-minute hedging, traders said.

Any activity that has been detected has been either minor position adjustment or related to dollar-driven events like the weekend Group of Seven (G7) finance ministers meeting and the slew of U.S. economic data due out later this week.

"After the G7 meeting, the UK election is almost a non-event. Politics are just not what's leading sterling around at the moment," said Frank Mikulecz, futures and options trader at Baxter Financial Services on Dublin's FINEX trading floor. A rise in UK interest rates is widely expected shortly after the election and this is likely regardless of the result, he said.

Mikulecz said there was some demand on Friday for short-dated out-of-the-money calls, the right to buy sterling futures, but this was more likely hedging against a post-G7 reaction than any sudden angst about the election outcome.
"We see more risk to the franc from the upcoming French elections than to sterling from next Thursday," he said.

One-month sterling/mark implied vol was today at 9.20/9.50 percent compared with 9.00/9.30 last week and unchanged from the previous Monday, April 14. One-month 25-delta risk reversals, the price difference between calls and puts, show a slight 0.0/0.4 bias to sterling puts on the mark from par last Monday.

With the UK deemed to be more in synch with the U.S. interest rate cycle than with continental Europe, sterling has been tracking the dollar's rise against the mark in recent months and rose close to a 4-1/2-year high against the German unit overnight.

For sterling/dollar, tight ranges remain intact and implied vols remains substantially lower than sterling/mark equivalents. One month vol was 7.20/7.60 percent, up slightly from 6.95/7.25 percent last Monday but unchanged from the previous Monday.
One-month cable risk reversals were also slightly biased to sterling puts at 0.1/0.4.

Weekend opinion polls showed the opposition Labour Party retaining a powerful lead of up to 20 percentage points over the ruling Conservatives. Labour has consistently held a double- digit lead in the polls for months.
If these polls were translated on average across the country, it would give Labour a majority of well over 100 seats in the new parliament.

Traders and analysts said a hint of uncertainty crept into the market after one survey last week showed the Labour lead as narrow as five points, but any poll since then has refuted such a swing and this suggests it was a one-off rogue result.
"We did see some pick-up in sterling hedging after the release of that poll last week," said Sara Sullivan, senior manager of global FX sales at HSBC Markets.
"Although most of the market still believes in a Labour victory, that showed there's still an outside risk of a hung parliament and this will keep vol bid through the week."

Currency analysts said the worst outcome for sterling would be a hung parliament, where no party gets an overall majority and economic policy could be effectively be paralysed for a protracted period of time.
Strategists, meantime, suggest different ways of positioning in the options market ahead of the election.

"If you look at any historical market reaction to well-discounted election outcomes, then the spot does very little but the implied vol declines," said Joe Prendergast, currency strategist at Merrill Lynch.
"If, as opinion polls suggest, Labour is set for a comfortable victory, then it would be better to be short sterling/mark vol regardless of the knee-jerk spot reaction."
Prendergast said one-month sterling/mark vol is well above Merrill's model of fair value, while cable vol is sub par.

As any surprise result would see an independent sterling reaction manifest itself more in cable than the cross, one good spread trade would be to be short sterling/mark vol but long cable vol, the Merrill strategist suggested.
